title: More Law Schools Embrace AI: Curriculum Integration Across Legal Education
author: Kathryn Palmer · Donna Campbell

st.t: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development

kp.k: AI adoption pressures law schools to prepare practice-ready graduates
kp.d: Palmer's 29 August 2025 article reports that some 30 percent of law offices use AI-based technology tools, citing ABA data published that spring. ChatGPT is described as the most widely used tool, alongside growing uptake of legal research-specific products. Linna reports rising employer expectations of graduates' AI exposure but cautions that many schools offer only basic training or less.
qs: some 30 percent of law offices are using AI-based technology tools
Law firms are starting to expect more and more that students will be exposed to this in law school,
But they also understand that the current reality is that not many law schools are doing much more than basic training. And some may not even be doing that.

kp.k: Curriculum uptake is widespread but depth remains questioned
kp.d: Palmer cites ABA figures that 62 percent of law schools have incorporated formal first-year opportunities to learn about or use AI, 93 percent are considering curriculum updates, and 55 percent of programs offered specialized AI courses in 2024. Perlman's suggestion that the last figure has increased is an assessment rather than updated survey evidence; Linna questions whether existing offerings are adequate.
qs: have incorporated formal opportunities to learn about or use AI into their first-year curriculum; 93 percent are considering updating their curriculum to incorporate AI education.
55 percent of programs offered specialized courses designed to teach students about AI in 2024
That percentage has likely increased over the past year, said Andrew Perlman

kp.k: AI education should preserve foundational expertise and human judgment
kp.d: The articles consistently frame AI as complementing rather than replacing lawyers' reasoning. Moon argues that intentional use requires foundational knowledge, while O'Leary emphasizes both student inputs and assessment of outputs. Reported fake citations and misquotes illustrate why access to tools alone is insufficient. Efficiency, accuracy and expanded public access to legal services are presented as expert expectations or potential benefits, not measured outcomes.
qs: At its best, experts believe AI has the power to make lawyers more efficient and accurate, as well as the potential to expand public access to legal services.
We have to preserve that core learning process so that they remain the human expert and this technology complements and supports their expertise.
The student must be the bread on both sides. What the student puts in, and how the output is assessed, matters more than the tool in the middle.

kp.k: Entry-level employment effects remain uncertain; AI familiarity may help
kp.d: Palmer identifies document review and legal research as traditional junior assignments in which AI tools excel, but explicitly says the employment impact over the next several years is unclear. The article reports 17 percent of legal-sector jobs potentially at risk as one interpretation of a Goldman Sachs report, not an established displacement outcome. Moon predicts an advantage for AI-familiar graduates and says innovative firms are investigating profitability benefits.
qs: It’s not clear yet the extent to which AI will reshape the legal job market over the next several years
17 percent of jobs in the legal sector may be at risk.
Law firms on the cutting edge of innovation are certainly trying to figure out how leveraging this technology improves their bottom line,
For recent graduates, those who are coming into firms with an understanding and familiarity with AI have a leg up.

kp.k: Marchant urges earlier acquisition of advanced associate skills
kp.d: Marchant argues that AI requires law schools and firms to change training so students acquire some third- and fourth-year associate skills before graduation. He describes existing AI capabilities as already transformative and predicts competitive replacement of lawyers unfamiliar with AI by those who understand it. Arizona State's AI specialization, begun the previous year, is reported as an institutional response.
qs: It creates a requirement for law schools and law firms to train future lawyers differently, so that they learn some of the third- and fourth-year associate skills while they’re still in law school,
Even if AI doesn’t advance any further, it’s already come so far that it’s transforming the practice of law, and it could change even more.

kp.k: USF adopts curriculum-wide AI education with industry partnerships
kp.d: Palmer describes the University of San Francisco School of Law as the country's first to integrate generative AI education throughout its curriculum, supported by partnerships with Accordance and Anthropic announced the preceding week. Dean Kalb argues that understanding AI is necessary across practice areas and anticipates changes in required lawyer tasks and skills as tools improve and specialize.
qs: the University of San Francisco School of Law to become the first in the country to integrate generative AI education throughout its curriculum.
Those efforts will be aided through partnerships with Accordance and Anthropic
AI is something every student needs to understand, no matter what kind of law they want to do,

kp.k: Suffolk combines required AI modules with critical output analysis
kp.d: Palmer reports a required custom generative AI learning track within first-year legal practice skills in fall 2025; Campbell describes required first-year AI instruction supported by Hotshot's asynchronous modules. The material introduces large language models before classroom editing and analysis of generated content. O'Leary emphasizes understanding uses and implications rather than becoming technology experts, including identifying missed counterarguments and defective legal writing. Campbell describes brainstorming and outlining as supported uses, while cautioning against reliance for final drafting or legal analysis.
qs: is requiring all first-year students to complete a custom generative AI learning track as part of its course on legal practice skills.
The goal is not for our students to become tech experts but to understand the usage and implication of AI in the legal profession.
There needs to be an understanding of why AI missed a counterargument or produced a junk rule paragraph.
These exercises help students learn that AI can support brainstorming and outlining but isn’t yet reliable for final drafting or legal analysis.

kp.k: Employer anecdote reinforces independent analytical competence
kp.d: Harvard second-year student Jacob Levine reports that his summer law-firm internship permitted AI but emphasized assessing his own analytical ability. His experience supports the articles' emphasis on combining tool familiarity with independent legal skills, but is an individual account rather than systematic employer evidence.
qs: AI was a tool that was present and using it was permitted, but there was a lot of emphasis on gauging the ability of the individual to be able to do the analytical work that’s expected of a young attorney,
It’s important to know how to use AI but not purely rely on it and use it blindly. A big part of being able to do that is knowing how to do everything yourself.

kp.k: Case Western mandates practical AI training for first-years
kp.d: Campbell reports that Case Western Reserve partnered with Wickard.ai to make AI training mandatory for its entire first-year class and available to the wider school community. Pre-class work, live instruction, guest speakers and hands-on prompting exercises encourage critical use. Cupar frames the initiative as practice readiness, analogizing AI's incorporation into legal work to Westlaw and Lexis's effects on research. General restrictions on AI drafting assignments coexist with faculty-guided exceptions.
qs: The program included pre-class assignments, live instruction, guest speakers and hands-on exercises.
Students practiced crafting prompts and experimenting with various AI platforms.

While CWRU Law, like many law schools, has general prohibitions against AI use in drafting assignments, faculty are encouraged to allow exceptions and to guide students in exploring AI’s capabilities responsibly.
Just like Westlaw and Lexis changed legal research, AI is going to be part of legal work going forward.

kp.k: WashU links AI verification to traditional research fundamentals
kp.d: Campbell states that, starting with the Class of 2025, WashU embeds generative AI instruction in a yearlong, one-credit first-year Legal Research course. Traditional authority, sources and research methods remain central. Hands-on work teaches students to check generated results for hallucinations and inaccuracies and compare them with traditional research. Hook argues that foundational research competence enables assessment of AI results, rather than AI replacing legal reasoning.
qs: Delivered as a yearlong, one-credit course, the revamped curriculum maintains a strong emphasis on core legal research fundamentals

Students receive hands-on training in legal-specific generative AI platforms and develop the skills needed to evaluate AI-generated results, detect hallucinated or inaccurate content, and compare outcomes with traditional research methods.
By teaching the basics, we teach the skills necessary to evaluate whether AI-produced legal research results are any good.

kp.k: Drake's certificate expands interdisciplinary AI and legal specialization
kp.d: Campbell reports a new AI Law Certificate for second- and third-year J.D. students drawing on computer science, art and justice-reform expertise. Its proposed topics extend beyond operational AI use to machine vision and trademark law, quantum computing and cybersecurity, and AI ethics and regulation. Dean Jones presents it as preparation for leadership across practice, government, nonprofit work, policymaking and academia, rather than reporting graduate outcomes.
qs: Designed for completion during a student’s second and third years, the certificate program emphasizes interdisciplinary collaboration
Students will engage with advanced topics such as machine vision and trademark law, quantum computing and cybersecurity, and the broader ethical and regulatory challenges posed by AI.
Artificial Intelligence is not just changing industries; it’s reshaping governance, ethics and the very framework of legal systems,

kp.k: AI simulations broaden negotiation and oral argument practice
kp.d: Suffolk's online platform provides text or voice negotiation practice with bots that change tactics, alongside an AI mock judge developed by the legal writing team and litigation lab. These tools are described as enabling realistic dialogue and real-time questioning of case theories beyond static materials. O'Leary reports pedagogical usefulness, particularly for students poorly served by reading outlines alone; no measured learning gains are provided.
qs: Unlike overly accommodating AI assistants, these bots shift tactics and strategies, mirroring the adaptive nature of real-world legal negotiators.
the AI mock judge engages students in real-time argument rehearsals, asking follow-up questions and testing their case theories.
It’s especially helpful for students who don’t get much out of reading their outline alone,

kp.k: Academic integrity restrictions face resource and equity tensions
kp.d: O'Leary notes uneven institutional resources for advanced AI teaching. Suffolk prohibits generative AI on assignments unless explicitly permitted by the professor, but she describes the policy as evolving. She questions complete prohibition on equity grounds because some students already receive assistance from lawyer relatives or paid tutors; this concerns educational access to assistance, not evidence of reduced unmet public legal need.
qs: Others don’t have the resources to do much at the upper level.
Suffolk Law has a default policy that prohibits use of generative AI on assignments unless a professor explicitly allows it.
You can’t ignore the equity issues,
To prohibit [AI] entirely is starting to feel unrealistic.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI is changing practice-readiness expectations and prompting curriculum reform; speakers predict an advantage for AI-literate lawyers while stressing that AI should complement, not replace, foundational legal expertise.
pts.d: Kathryn Palmer reports increasing AI adoption in law offices and legal education. Daniel W. Linna Jr. says employers increasingly expect graduates to have AI exposure, but many schools offer only basic training or less. Caitlin Moon predicts a competitive advantage for AI-familiar graduates; Gary Marchant argues that schools must teach some skills traditionally acquired in the third and fourth associate years and predicts that AI-knowledgeable lawyers will replace those without that knowledge. Andrew Perlman likewise predicts improved long-term prospects from combining traditional practice skills with AI capability. Palmer describes greater efficiency, accuracy and public access to legal services as potential benefits attributed to experts, rather than established outcomes. She explicitly leaves the extent of job-market change unresolved and reports a secondary interpretation that 17 percent of legal jobs may be at risk. Donna Campbell describes AI-assisted brainstorming, outlining, negotiation practice and oral-argument rehearsal, while stating that AI is not yet reliable for final drafting or legal analysis. Jennifer Cupar predicts that AI will become a continuing part of legal work. Roscoe Jones Jr. makes a broader claim that AI is reshaping governance, ethics and legal systems.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The articles support adoption claims with ABA data and institutional examples; employment and transformation predictions largely rest on expert opinion, alongside a secondary report interpretation and one student’s internship experience.
pts.d: Palmer cites ABA data indicating approximately 30 percent of law offices use AI-based tools, 62 percent of law schools have formal first-year AI learning opportunities, 93 percent are considering curriculum updates, and 55 percent offered specialized AI courses in 2024. These are adoption measures, not measured effects on employment or service quality. She supports the need for responsible use by referring to fabricated citations and misquotes in legal filings, without providing a measured hallucination rate. The reported 17 percent jobs-at-risk figure is attributed to one interpretation of a Goldman Sachs report, not to an observed displacement study; the linked URL contains a different numerical framing, so the supplied text does not resolve that figure. Concrete curriculum examples include USF’s curriculum-wide integration, Suffolk’s required first-year learning track and simulations, CWRU’s mandatory first-year training, WashU’s research instruction and Drake’s certificate. Jacob Levine’s internship account illustrates an employer permitting AI while assessing independent analytical ability. Claims about employment advantages, accelerated skill requirements and institutional transformation are attributed to interviewed educators; no comparative hiring, learning-outcome or productivity results are supplied. O’Leary’s descriptions of negotiation bots and a mock judge provide practitioner testimony about their educational usefulness.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The articles describe changes underway in 2024–2025 and uncertain employment effects over the next several years; benefits depend on critical use, verification and retained human expertise.
pts.d: Campbell’s article is dated July 9, 2025, and Palmer’s August 29, 2025. Palmer uses 2024 curriculum data and reports Suffolk’s requirement for the coming fall; Perlman’s suggestion that specialized offerings increased over the preceding year is an estimate, not an updated count. Marchant says existing AI capability already changes practice even if development stops, while Kalb expects further improvements and specialization to alter lawyers’ required skills. Palmer explicitly says the scale of legal employment change over the next several years remains unclear. Moon conditions responsible adoption on preserving core learning and human expertise; Levine emphasizes being able to perform the work independently. Campbell’s qualification that AI is not yet reliable for final drafting or analysis concerns current capability, not a permanent limit. WashU’s approach requires students to check AI results for fabricated or inaccurate material and compare them with traditional research. Suffolk generally prohibits AI on assignments without express permission; CWRU also permits faculty-guided exceptions to general drafting restrictions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are students, junior lawyers, employers and legal educators; the articles also identify potential public-access benefits and equity issues among students.
pts.d: Students and recent graduates face expectations to combine independent legal reasoning with competent AI use. Junior lawyers are particularly implicated because document review and legal research have traditionally formed part of entry-level work. Innovative law firms are exploring financial benefits and employers increasingly value combined traditional and AI skills. Law schools and faculty face pressure to revise curricula, introduce practical exercises and balance AI exposure with foundational learning, sometimes with limited resources. Kalb presents AI understanding as relevant across practice areas. Drake’s program targets careers in private practice, government, nonprofits, policymaking and academia. The public is identified as a potential beneficiary of expanded legal-service access, but the articles do not document access-to-justice outcomes. O’Leary raises student equity concerns because some students already receive help from family lawyers or paid tutors, making a blanket AI prohibition seem increasingly unrealistic to her.
